 Subscribe Home Our Region Business Sports Steelers Food & Drink Obituaries Public Notices PGe Edition Breaking Criminal Justice Monaca man charged with stealing more than $1 million in Federal Student Aid refunds through ‘ghost student’ accounts 
 Stephana Ocneanu 11/20/2026 2:03 p.m. EST Share Share this via... A federal grand jury in Pittsburgh indicted a Monaca man for allegedly stealing more than $1 million in Federal Student Aid refunds. ( Micha? Chodyra / Getty Images ) Emmanuel Hilton, 29, was indicted on six money laundering charges and one charge for the conspiracy to commit wire fraud
 A federal grand jury in Pittsburgh has indicted a Monaca man for allegedly stealing more than $1 million in Federal Student Aid refunds by using the names of identity theft victims, U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti announced Friday.
 Emmanuel Hilton, 29, was named as the sole defendant in a seven-count indictment filed on Wednesday. He faces six charges of money laundering and one conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge.
 The indictment alleges that Hilton acted as a “money mule” from June 2023 through February 2026, opening multiple bank accounts for the purpose of receiving FSA refund dollars and electronically transferring them to co-conspirators in Kenya.
 He received around $1,065,048 through these efforts, according to court documents. 
 Advertise with us The indictment came out of an investigation conducted by the FBI and the U.S. Department of Education Office of Inspector General. 
 Beginning in late 2021, the Department of Education began receiving reports from multiple universities and colleges in California of an “excessive” number of student enrollment requests and a variety of “unusual” patterns associated with the student registrations, according to the indictment. 
 The department analyzed data from the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or FAFSA, system and found the same physical address was used for multiple students. It also identified overlapping patterns in creating similar usernames and passwords.
 The accounts appeared to be created using the stolen personally identifiable information of actual U.S. citizens.
 At least four victims were identified to the grand jury. Two reside in California, one in Oklahoma and one in Minnesota.
 Advertise with us Schools outside of California were also identified throughout the course of the investigation.
 “Once a FAFSA account was created, the fraud actors would enroll in a university or community college using the names of actual U.S. citizens. There were no actual students — either online or in person — and the fake enrollees were referred to as ‘ghost students,” the indictment stated. 
 In cases where the department awarded a grant or issued a loan in the ghost student’s name, the funds would be sent to the school — which would then subtract from the tuition and fees owed and refund the remaining amount back to the ghost student, typically via electronic funds to a bank account that was managed by Hilton.
 The conspirators would “cause the disenrollment” of the ghost student, according to the indictment.
 The conspiracy involved perpetrators inside and outside the U.S. and relied “heavily” on the use of interstate and foreign wire communications, according to court documents.
 Advertise with us For the wire fraud charge, Hilton could be sentenced to up to 20 years in prison and/or be required to pay a fine of more than $250,000 or twice the gross pecuniary gain – the total money gained from the offense before deducting expenses or costs.
 Each of the six money laundering charges carry a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison and/or a fine of more than $250,000 or twice the amount of funds tied to the crimes. 
 Assistant U.S. Attorney Brendan J. McKenna is prosecuting this case on behalf of the government.
 Stephana Ocneanu 
 socneanu@post-gazette.com
